title: Valley-Enabled Intrinsic Dresselhaus Spin-Orbit Coupling in Silicon
authors: Johannes L. P. Steinschuld, Hendrik J. Bluhm, Lars R. Schreiber, Seyed Akbar Jafari
abstract: We develop a symmetry-based theory of spin-orbit-valley coupling in silicon that reveals an intrinsic source of Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling independent of interfaces or external electric fields. Treating the valley degree of freedom as a symmetry-carrying quantum degree of freedom, we show that the Dresselhaus interaction is necessarily valley off-diagonal and that a bulk contribution proportional to the valley Pauli matrix $τ_1$ is symmetry allowed. Tight-binding calculations yield a bulk coupling more than an order of magnitude larger than typical interface-induced spin-orbit coupling; achieving the same energy scale through the interface-induced mechanism would require electric fields roughly 50 times larger than typical fields. We further derive the symmetry-allowed spin-valley couplings generated by magnetic-field gradients and show how they account for the valley-dependent Zeeman splitting observed in micromagnet experiments. A slight tilt of the background magnetic field out of the plane produces an additional isotropic contribution linear in $B_z$, providing an experimentally accessible signature of the corresponding coupling constant. Finally, we predict a spin-independent micromagnet-induced valley splitting in the $τ_3$ channel, which is distinct from the $τ_{1,2}$ channels generated by alloy disorder and therefore remains robust against disorder-induced cancellation. These results establish valley symmetry as a fundamental ingredient in the spin-orbit physics of silicon and provide new mechanisms for controlling and probing spin and valley degrees of freedom in silicon quantum devices.
summary: This paper establishes a symmetry-based theory for spin-orbit-valley coupling in silicon, revealing a strong, intrinsic Dresselhaus SOC that does not require interfaces or external fields. By treating the valley degree of freedom as a fundamental quantum variable, the authors predict measurable, robust signatures of valley-dependent spin splitting using techniques like magnetic field gradients.
main_problem: To develop a symmetry-based theory characterizing the intrinsic source of Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in silicon, independent of interfaces or external electric fields.
main_result: The theory reveals a bulk, intrinsic Dresselhaus SOC that is necessarily valley off-diagonal and significantly larger than typical interface-induced couplings. It also predicts robust, disorder-resistant valley splitting mechanisms.
method: The authors employed symmetry analysis using the double X group and tight-binding calculations to construct symmetry-allowed Hamiltonians incorporating spin and valley degrees of freedom.
model_or_system: The system is bulk silicon, modeled by incorporating spin ($\sigma$) and valley ($	au$) degrees of freedom. The analysis treats the valley degree of freedom as a symmetry-carrying quantum degree of freedom.
key_observables: Valley-dependent Zeeman splitting ($\Delta	au E_Z$), spin-orbit-valley (SOV) coupling terms, and the $	au_3$ channel splitting.
important_parameters: The intrinsic bulk Dresselhaus coupling is predicted to be $>1$ order of magnitude larger than interface-induced SOC; the analysis involves magnetic field gradients and external fields ($B_z$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the structure of the double X group and the assumption that the SOC terms must be even under time-reversal (TR) symmetry.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the two valleys in bulk Si and show spin textures for SOC effects; Tables list permissible spin-orbit terms and couplings.
paper_structure: The paper systematically builds the Hamiltonian using symmetry constraints, first identifying the intrinsic bulk Dresselhaus term, then analyzing how magnetic field gradients induce valley-dependent corrections to the Zeeman splitting, and finally predicting a robust $	au_3$ splitting mechanism.
why_interesting: This work provides a fundamental theoretical framework linking crystal symmetry (valley degree of freedom) directly to spin-orbit coupling, offering new, intrinsic mechanisms for controlling spin and valley qubits in silicon quantum devices.
